overview: The Teutonic Order combined a religious community, military organization and Baltic territorial rule. Its conquests imposed Christian rule on Baltic peoples, while its castles contained kitchens, offices, music rooms and ingenious heating. This map joins Prussian and Livonian territories whose political histories differed; many everyday details come from Malbork.

periods.title: Hospital origins and Baltic expansion
periods.summary: A hospital community near Acre developed into the Order. Its later Baltic conquests created a territorial power; the map record begins only in 1279.

periods.title: Malbork and the Baltic branches
periods.summary: The grand master moved to Malbork in 1309. Prussia and the Order’s Livonian branch belonged to a wider organization, but Livonia also contained other centres of power.

periods.title: Different regional endings
periods.summary: Prussian monastic rule became a secular duchy in 1525. The Livonian branch’s transformation followed in 1561, after this imported map interval ends.

sections.title: Warm rooms and a very unusual bathroom

items.text: Malbork’s Gdanisko tower served as the castle’s main medieval toilet. Its arches let water flow underneath and carry waste away. The journey to the bathroom was part of a carefully planned system, complete with a substantial tower.

The same tower could serve as a final defensive refuge. At first, part of its wooden connecting passage could be raised; later builders replaced the passage with a permanent masonry corridor. A toilet that doubled as a last defensive refuge gives “occupied” an unusually serious meaning.

Furnaces heated fieldstones, which stored warmth and released it through channels into the rooms above. This helped heat large spaces while conserving scarce local firewood. The castle’s comfort depended on masonry, airflow and somebody keeping the fire going.

Ceramic or metal covers over the floor openings regulated the heat entering the room. Adjusting a cover was the medieval version of changing the heating setting. Many surviving furnaces were rebuilt in the nineteenth century, so today’s visible equipment includes later restoration.

Archaeological work at the castle’s research centre uncovered another heat-storage furnace, described by the museum as one of the earliest surviving examples there. The museum report does not give it a precise date. Discoveries beneath later buildings can add a new chapter to the history of keeping warm.

Meals for the Great Refectory came from a neighboring kitchen with a large hearth beneath a powerful chimney hood. A small cook’s room and a store stood nearby. Impressive dining halls needed practical workspaces, ingredients and cooks behind the scenes.

Painted draperies decorate the cook’s chamber today, but the museum dates them to the early twentieth century. They belong to the castle’s restoration story. Looking closely at a historic room means distinguishing medieval fabric from the choices of later decorators.

In the convent’s common room, knights spent some free time listening to music from a gallery along the north wall. The setting provided a shared place to relax. Even a community famous for armor and fortifications had occasions when the important equipment was musical.

The infirmary cared for aged and weakened knights. It had its own dining room, chapel and bath, bringing meals, worship and washing close to residents who needed support. These arrangements describe care within the castle’s religious community.

A sickroom adjoined the infirmary dining hall, with a toilet in a nearby annex. The museum also identifies later alterations, including stained glass installed in 1918. The rooms combine traces of medieval care with centuries of reuse.

The Order’s financial officer had a suite containing living space, a treasury and a servant’s room. Surviving mill equipment is displayed near the convent kitchen. Money, grain and household labor supported the castle as surely as its walls did.

Malbork was built on an exceptional scale in Gothic brick. Its later conservators developed careful recording and restoration methods; those records helped reconstruction after severe damage in the Second World War. What survives reflects both medieval builders and people who studied their work centuries later.

A short Latin writing sample is “Chronicon Prussiae”, meaning “Chronicle of Prussia”. This is the title of the 1679 printed edition of Peter of Dusburg’s medieval chronicle preserved by the Bavarian State Library. The witness is a later printed book, not the author’s original manuscript.

Livonia had several centres of power; the Order’s local branch was the strongest, rather than the only authority. In 1561 its last master, Gotthard Kettler, became Duke of Courland and Semigallia after an agreement with the Polish-Lithuanian ruler. This northern story continued after Prussia’s separate transformation.

ending.text: In 1525 Albert adopted Lutheranism, made the Order’s Prussian lands a secular duchy and paid homage to the Polish king. The Livonian branch followed a different path to its 1561 settlement. The religious Order continued elsewhere. The imported 1530 cutoff is therefore neither the end of every branch nor the disappearance of Baltic communities.
